claim: Previous studies have demonstrated the importance of the primary sensory cortex for the detection, discrimination, and awareness of visual stimuli.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated the importance of the primary sensory cortex for the detection, discrimination, and awareness of visual stimuli
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research in the field.

claim: It is unknown how neuronal populations in the primary sensory cortex process detected and undetected stimuli differently.
source: but it is unknown how neuronal populations in this area process detected and undetected stimuli differently
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current knowledge based on the literature.

claim: Visual detection correlates more strongly with population response heterogeneity rather than overall response strength.
source: we found that visual detection correlates more strongly with population response heterogeneity rather than overall response strength
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Neuronal populations showed consistencies in activation patterns across temporally spaced trials in association with hit responses, but not during nondetections.
source: Moreover, neuronal populations showed consistencies in activation patterns across temporally spaced trials in association with hit responses, but not during nondetections.
evidence: This finding is based on experimental observations from the study.

claim: Detection depends on transient differentiation in neuronal activity within cortical populations.
source: these results suggest that detection depends on transient differentiation in neuronal activity within cortical populations
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results presented in the study.

claim: Lesion studies in humans and animals indicate the causal importance of the primary visual cortex (V1) in detection, discrimination, and awareness of visual stimuli.
source: Lesion studies in humans and animals indicate the causal importance of the primary visual cortex (V1) in detection, discrimination, and awareness of visual stimuli (Lashley, 1943; Weiskrantz et al., 1974; Weiskrantz, 1996)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to historical lesion studies.

claim: Direct optogenetic inhibition of mouse V1 confirms its role in visual detection.
source: this role has been recently confirmed by direct optogenetic inhibition of mouse V1 (Glickfeld et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a recent optogenetic study.

claim: Visual perception has been proposed to arise from interactions between stimulus-specific processing in V1 and neural activity in higher visual and frontoparietal areas.
source: Visual perception has been proposed to arise from interactions between stimulus-specific processing in V1 and neural activity in higher visual and frontoparietal areas, involving both feed-forward propagation of activity and recurrent, top-down feedback (Shadlen and Newsome, 1996; Britten and van Wezel, 1998; Lamme et al., 2000; Haynes et al., 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to theoretical and experimental work.

claim: The intensity, duration, and reproducibility of sensory neural activity may provide signatures critical for visual perception.
source: it has been suggested that the intensity, duration, and reproducibility of sensory neural activity may provide signatures critical for visual perception (e.g. Moutoussis and Zeki, 2002; Schurger et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research proposing these mechanisms.

claim: Neural activity in V1 does not correlate with visual perception because stimuli that were seen or not seen evoked similar V1 blood-oxygenation-level-dependent signals.
source: it has been proposed that neural activity in V1 does not correlate with visual perception because stimuli that were seen or not seen evoked similar V1 blood-oxygenation-level-dependent signals (Vuilleumier et al., 2001; Rees, 2000)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to fMRI studies.

claim: The proposal that V1 activity does not correlate with visual perception remains an area of substantial controversy.
source: but this remains an area of substantial controversy (Ress and Heeger, 2003; Palmer et al., 2007; Nienborg and Cumming, 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies presenting conflicting evidence.

claim: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), electro-encephalogram (EEG), and magnetoencephalography (MEG) rely on a mean-field approach.
source: it is important to recall that functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), electro-encephalogram (EEG), and magnetoencephalography (MEG) rely on a mean-field approach
evidence: This is a statement about the technical characteristics of these measurement methods.

claim: Neural correlates of perception may be coded in more subtle ways that take into account the local differentiation present in populations of sensory neurons.
source: leaving open the possibility that neural correlates of perception may be coded in more subtle ways that take into account the local differentiation present in populations of sensory neurons
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on limitations of mean-field approaches.

claim: Local, functional differentiation is supported by single- or multiunit recording studies in visual, auditory, and somatosensory areas of animals trained to make perceptual decisions.
source: Such local, functional differentiation is supported by single- or multiunit recording studies in visual, auditory, and somatosensory areas of animals trained to make perceptual decisions (Logothetis et al., 1995; Britten et al., 1996; Posner and Gilbert, 1999; Petersen, 2002; Luna et al., 2005; Palmer et al., 2007; Mitchell et al., 2009; Cohen and Maunsell, 2009; Cohen and Maunsell, 2011; Sachidhanandam et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2013; Miyashita and Feldman, 2013; Doron et al., 2014; McGinley et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by extensive citations to electrophysiological studies.

claim: Shared response variability between neurons (noise correlation) might be particularly important for sensory processing because noise correlations can influence the amount of information that can be extracted from neuronal population codes.
source: it has become clear that the shared response variability between neurons (i.e. noise correlation) might be particularly important for sensory processing because noise correlations can influence the amount of information that can be extracted from neuronal population codes (Averbeck et al., 2006; Cafaro and Rieke, 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical and experimental work on noise correlations.

claim: Noise correlations can be reduced during stimulus presentation and directed attention, which may aid in disentangling stimulus information from noisy population responses.
source: it has been observed that these correlations can be reduced during stimulus presentation (Gutnisky and Dragoi, 2008; Snyder et al., 2014) and directed attention, which may aid in disentangling stimulus information from noisy population responses (Mitchell et al., 2009; Cohen and Maunsell, 2009; Herrero et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on attention and noise correlations.

claim: Noise correlations have the drawback of not being an instantaneous measure—their computation requires integrating neural activity over multiple time points or stimulus repetitions.
source: Although noise correlations have been studied well, they have the drawback of not being an instantaneous measure—their computation requires integrating neural activity over multiple time points or stimulus repetitions.
evidence: This is a statement about the computational properties of noise correlations.

claim: Instantaneous aspects of population activity in cortex, such as temporal spike co-occurrence and population sparseness, seem critical for efficient neural coding.
source: Instantaneous aspects of population activity in cortex, such as temporal spike co-occurrence and population sparseness, seem critical for efficient neural coding (Olshausen and Field, 1997; Vinje, 2000; Benucci et al., 2013; Harris and Mrsic-Flogel, 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical and experimental work on neural coding.

claim: Measures based on the variability and correlations between neurons correlate better with the animal's decision than simpler approaches based on the mean spiking rate.
source: It has, for example, been shown that measures based on the variability and correlations between neurons correlate better with the animal's decision than simpler approaches based on the mean spiking rate (Safaai et al., 2013; Carnevale et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies in somatosensory and auditory cortex.

claim: In the domain of visual perception the behavioral relevance of only few population measures has been experimentally tested in paradigms where animals report behaviorally whether they have seen a stimulus or not.
source: However, in the domain of visual perception the behavioral relevance of only few population measures has been experimentally tested in paradigms where animals report behaviorally whether they have seen a stimulus or not.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in the literature regarding visual perception studies.

claim: The authors investigated correlates of visual stimulus detection using two-photon calcium imaging of populations of ~100 neurons in V1 L2/3 of mice performing a detection task.
source: Therefore, we investigated correlates of visual stimulus detection using two-photon calcium imaging of populations of ~100 neurons in V1 L2/3 of mice performing a detection task
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Superficial layers are easy to access with calcium imaging and have been reported to show neural correlates with stimulus detection.
source: as superficial layers are easy to access with calcium imaging and have been reported to show neural correlates with stimulus detection (van der Togt, 2006; Ito and Gilbert, 1999)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies and practical considerations.

claim: The authors developed a novel population metric—response heterogeneity—that correlates better with stimulus detection performance, and particularly with the animal's reaction time, than traditional measures.
source: This led us to develop a novel population metric—response heterogeneity—that correlates better with stimulus detection performance, and particularly with the animal's reaction time, than traditional measures by capturing the dissimilarity of neuronal responses within a population.
evidence: This describes a key methodological contribution and finding of the study.

claim: An assumption in many computational models of vision is that neurons in distributed cortical architectures have relatively fixed roles in encoding visual features, but modulate their activation in a temporally dynamic manner based on attentional needs that can influence perception.
source: Second, an assumption in many computational models of vision is that neurons in distributed cortical architectures have relatively fixed roles in encoding visual features, but modulate their activation in a temporally dynamic manner based on attentional needs that can influence perception (e.g. Jones and Palmer, 1987; Itti et al., 1998; Desimone, 1998; Dayan and Abbott, 2001; Deco and Rolls, 2004; Reynolds and Heeger, 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to computational models of vision.

claim: Visual stimulus detection does not correlate well with mean response strength, but is significantly correlated with population heterogeneity.
source: We report that (1) visual stimulus detection does not correlate well with mean response strength, but is significantly correlated with population heterogeneity
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: Neuronal populations show consistencies in activation patterns across temporally spaced trials in association with hit responses, but not when the animal fails to report a stimulus.
source: (2) neuronal populations show consistencies in activation patterns across temporally spaced trials in association with hit responses, but not when the animal fails to report a stimulus
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: In addition to heterogeneity, multidimensional structures in neuronal population responses provide information on visual detection.
source: (3) in addition to heterogeneity, multidimensional structures in neuronal population responses provide information on visual detection
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: Mice were trained to perform a go/no-go stimulus detection task where they indicated by licking whether a square-wave drifting grating was presented.
source: animals were awake, head-fixed, and performed a detection task where they indicated by licking whether a square-wave drifting grating was presented
evidence: This describes the behavioral task used in the study.

claim: Stimulus duration was delimited by the onset of the first licking response, with a maximum of 3.0 s for no response.
source: Stimulus duration was delimited by the onset of the first licking response, with a maximum of 3.0 s for no response
evidence: This describes a methodological detail of the experimental design.

claim: No licks occurred during presentation of the stimulus.
source: therefore, no licks occurred during presentation of the stimulus
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental design where stimulus offset was triggered by licking.

claim: Test stimuli were presented with different luminance contrasts: 0.5%, 2%, 8%, and 32%.
source: we presented test stimuli with different luminance contrasts: 0.5%, 2%, 8%, and 32%
evidence: This describes the stimulus parameters used in the study.

claim: Test trials were interleaved with 0% no-contrast and 100% full-contrast probe trials to estimate the animals' ratio of false alarms and omissions due to lack of motivation.
source: These test trials were interleaved with 0% no-contrast and 100% full-contrast probe trials to estimate the animals' ratio of false alarms and omissions due to lack of motivation.
evidence: This describes the experimental design for controlling behavioral performance.

claim: Trials where animals responded within 150 ms after stimulus onset were discarded because such fast responses may be ascribed to spontaneous licking.
source: For all analyses, we discarded trials where animals responded within 150 ms after stimulus onset (0.3–3.5% of trials per animal) because such fast responses may be ascribed to spontaneous licking.
evidence: This describes a data exclusion criterion based on reasoning about behavioral confounds.

claim: All eight animals performed statistically significant stimulus detection during neural recordings.
source: All eight animals performed statistically significant stimulus detection during neural recordings, as quantified by non-overlapping 2.5th–97.5th Clopper–Pearson (CP) percentile confidence intervals (95% CI) (p<0.05) of behavioral response proportions for 0% and 100% contrast probe trials.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1c and described in the text with statistical analysis.

claim: Animals showed significant increases in behavioral response proportion with higher stimulus contrasts.
source: Animals showed significant increases in behavioral response (behav. resp.) proportion (linear regression analysis, see 'Materials and methods', p<0.001)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1e with statistical analysis.

claim: Animals showed reductions in reaction time with higher stimulus contrasts.
source: and reductions in reaction time (p<0.01)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1f with statistical analysis.

claim: The mean response increased with higher stimulus contrasts.
source: As expected, the mean response increased with higher stimulus contrasts
evidence: This is an observation from the data that matches expectations.

claim: For an example animal, there was no significant difference between hit and miss trials for any individual contrast in mean preferred population response.
source: However, for this animal we did not find a significant difference between hit and miss trials for any individual contrast [false-discovery rate (FDR)-corrected paired t-test, p>0.05 for all contrasts]
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: For both false alarms and correct rejections V1 mean population response was indistinguishable from zero.
source: (note that for both false alarms and correct rejections V1 mean population response was indistinguishable from zero; Figure 2c,d, 0% contrast; Figure 2—figure supplement 1a)
evidence: This is shown in the figures and described in the text.

claim: When grouping the test contrasts (0.5–32%), the data showed a modestly higher response for hit than miss trials for single animals as well as across animals.
source: When grouping the test contrasts (0.5–32%), the data did show a modestly higher response for hit than miss trials for single animals as well as across animals (p<0.05)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: Hit-associated increase in neural activity can be partly explained by specific neurons showing consistent dF/F0 increases or decreases across trials.
source: The hit-associated increase in neural activity per neuron for all hit trials of test contrast stimuli (panel I) can be partly explained by specific neurons showing consistent dF/F0 increases or decreases across trials (panel II)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2e and described in the text.

claim: Hit-associated increase in neural activity can be partly explained by trial-by-trial population-wide fluctuations regardless of neuronal identity.
source: partly by trial-by-trial population-wide fluctuations regardless of neuronal identity (panel III)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2e and described in the text.

claim: Hit modulation was explained to a small but significant extent by neuronal identity.
source: Hit modulation was explained to a small but significant extent by neuronal identity [R2=0.059; p<0.05; Figure 2e,f]
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis shown in the figure.

claim: Hit modulation was explained to a larger extent by population fluctuations across trials.
source: and to a larger extent by population fluctuations across trials [R2=0.248; Figure 2e(III)]
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis shown in the figure.

claim: The number of consistently hit-modulated neurons was significantly above chance.
source: The number of consistently hit-modulated neurons (which could be either up- or downregulated) was significantly above chance (Figure 2f; p<0.05)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis shown in the figure.

claim: Hit modulations could be explained with above-chance accuracy by neuron identity, population fluctuations, or both in 7/8, 8/8, and 8/8 animals, respectively.
source: This pattern was robust over animals as hit modulations could be explained with above-chance accuracy by neuron identity, population fluctuations, or both in 7/8, 8/8, and 8/8 animals, respectively (Figure 2g)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis shown in the figure.

claim: The fraction of significantly hit-modulated neurons was above chance (at p<0.05) for 7/8 animals.
source: The fraction of significantly hit-modulated neurons was above chance (at p<0.05) for 7/8 animals.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: The variance explained by the consistency of neuronal responses was fairly low (always R2<0.1).
source: Although significant for most subjects, the variance explained by the consistency of neuronal responses was fairly low (always R2<0.1)
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the data analysis.

claim: The combination of trial-by-trial population fluctuations and neuronal identity never exceeded R2=0.35.
source: and even the combination of trial-by-trial population fluctuations and neuronal identity never exceeded R2=0.35
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the data analysis.

claim: Detection-related neural correlates in V1 may be minor or a simple enhancement of mean activity is an index ill-suited to describe potentially strong, but more complex changes in neuronal population dynamics.
source: This could indicate either that detection-related neural correlates in V1 are minor or that a simple enhancement of mean activity is an index ill-suited to describe potentially strong, but more complex changes in neuronal population dynamics.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the low R2 values observed.

claim: Correlates of stimulus detection may be unfolding by multineuron interactions at the single trial level and rely on the relative contrast in activation between neurons.
source: In particular, we hypothesized that correlates of stimulus detection may be unfolding by multineuron interactions at the single trial level and rely on the relative contrast in activation between neurons.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their observations.

claim: The authors developed an alternative measure of population heterogeneity that aims to capture the spread in normalized population activity.
source: Therefore, we developed an alternative measure of population heterogeneity that aims to capture the spread in normalized population activity (Figure 3a,b; see also 'Materials and methods')
evidence: This describes a methodological contribution of the study.

claim: Population heterogeneity incorporates both trial-by-trial fluctuations and intra-population differences in a neuronal pairwise manner.
source: Therefore, population heterogeneity incorporates both trial-by-trial fluctuations and intra-population differences in a neuronal pairwise manner.
evidence: This describes a property of the heterogeneity metric.

claim: A neuron's contribution to heterogeneity is scaled to its relative level of activation and to its signal-to-noise ratio.
source: Its dependence on z-scored activity means that a neuron's contribution to heterogeneity is scaled to its relative level of activation—and because highly active neurons are often highly variable (Baddeley et al., 1997; Montijn et al., 2014) also to its signal-to-noise ratio.
evidence: This describes a property of the heterogeneity metric with citations to support the relationship between activity and variability.

claim: In an example animal, population activity heterogeneity shows a strong correlation with visual detection.
source: Population activity heterogeneity in an example animal shows a strong correlation with visual detection. Comparison between detected (resp.) and undetected (no resp.) trials for test contrasts as a group (paired t-test, p<0.001) was highly significant.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3c with statistical analysis.

claim: Across all animals, stimulus detection correlated with higher heterogeneity.
source: Stimulus detection correlated with higher heterogeneity; test contrast group hit–miss comparison was highly significant (p<0.001)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3d with statistical analysis.

claim: Hit–miss differences were found in the preferred population and nonpreferred population similar to the whole population.
source: Hit–miss differences were found in the preferred population (test contrast group, p<0.01) and nonpreferred population (test contrast group, p<0.01) similar to the whole population (d)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3e with statistical analysis.

claim: Heterogeneity showed a stronger correlation with stimulus detection than mean dF/F0 within the whole population, preferred population, and nonpreferred population.
source: Using a measure of effect size analysis (Cohen's d), heterogeneity was found to show a stronger correlation with stimulus detection than mean dF/F0 within the whole population (Cohen's d=0.114 vs. d=0.218); within the preferred population (Cohen's d=0.119 vs. d=0.213) and within the nonpreferred population (Cohen's d=0.110 vs. d=0.206) [paired t-tests over animals (n=8) whole population; p<0.05, preferred population; p<0.05, nonpreferred population; p<0.01]
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3f with statistical analysis.

claim: Both mean dF/F0 and heterogeneity predict the animal's response above chance.
source: Both measures predict the animal's response above chance (FDR-corrected paired t-test dF/F0 and heterogeneity AUC vs. 0.5, p<0.05 and p<0.001, respectively)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3h with statistical analysis.

claim: Behavior can be predicted better using heterogeneity than mean dF/F0.
source: but behavior can be predicted better using heterogeneity (paired t-test, dF/F0 vs. heterogeneity AUC, p<0.01)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3h with statistical analysis.

claim: Correlates of visual detection are better captured by the strength of pairwise response dissimilarities within the neuronal population than to overall increases in mean activation.
source: These results show that correlates of visual detection are better captured by the strength of pairwise response dissimilarities within the neuronal population than to overall increases in mean activation
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data analysis.

claim: Reaction time shows no correlation with mean preferred population dF/F0 activity during stimulus presentation for any individual animal nor for the meta-analysis over animals.
source: Reaction time shows no correlation with mean preferred population dF/F0 activity during stimulus presentation for any individual animal (left panel; example animal) nor for the meta-analysis over animals (right panel; FDR-corrected one sample t-test over individual regression slopes per animal, n=8, n.s.)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4a with statistical analysis.

claim: Heterogeneity shows a strong correlation with reaction time for an example animal as well as for the meta-analysis over animals.
source: Heterogeneity shows a strong correlation with reaction time (left panel; example animal, p<0.001) as well as well for the meta-analysis over animals (p<0.001)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4b with statistical analysis.

claim: Only heterogeneity and spread (SD) in instantaneous Pearson-like correlation correlate significantly with reaction time.
source: Only heterogeneity (FDR-corrected one sample t-test, p<0.001) and spread (SD) in instantaneous Pearson-like correlation (see 'Materials and methods') (p<0.01) correlate significantly with reaction time
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4c with statistical analysis.

claim: Heterogeneity explains more reaction-time-dependent variance than any other metric.
source: Heterogeneity explains more reaction-time-dependent variance than any other metric (FDR-corrected paired t-tests, all p<0.05)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4c with statistical analysis.

claim: When the animal has detected the stimulus, the decoder is better able to correctly judge its presence.
source: When the animal has detected the stimulus (resp.; green line), the decoder is better able to correctly judge its presence (a value of 1 indicates perfect performance, paired t-test, p<0.001)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4d with statistical analysis.

claim: Behavioral detection performance is more similar to the optimal decoder's performance than expected by chance.
source: Behavioral detection performance is more similar (sim.) to the optimal decoder's performance than expected by chance (paired t-test, n=8 animals, shuffled vs. real similarity, p<0.001)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4e with statistical analysis.

claim: Stimulus features (orientation, contrast) were better decodable when the animal made a correct detection.
source: additional analyses revealed that stimulus features (orientation, contrast) were better decodable when the animal made a correct detection (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a)
evidence: This is shown in the supplementary figure with analysis.

claim: Stimulus features were better decodable when heterogeneity was high.
source: and when heterogeneity was high (Figure 4—figure supplement 2b–d)
evidence: This is shown in the supplementary figure with analysis.

claim: Stimulus features, such as orientation, are represented more accurately by neuronal populations in V1 during hit trials, even though the specific orientation was irrelevant for the animal to perform the visual stimulus detection task.
source: Thus, stimulus features, such as orientation, are represented more accurately by neuronal populations in V1 during hit trials, even though the specific orientation was irrelevant for the animal to perform the visual stimulus detection task.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the decoding analysis.

claim: Neuromodulators such as acetylcholine (ACh) and noradrenaline are correlated with attention and arousal, and may influence cortical population dynamics.
source: Neuromodulators such as acetylcholine (ACh) and noradrenaline are correlated with attention and arousal, and may influence cortical population dynamics (Metherate et al., 1992; Coull et al., 2004; Pinto et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on neuromodulators.

claim: Using pre-stimulus-onset heterogeneity, fast response trials were highly predictable.
source: Using pre-stimulus-onset heterogeneity, fast response trials were highly predictable (FDR-corrected one-sample t-tests, p<0.01)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: Slow versus miss trials were not predictable using pre-stimulus-onset heterogeneity.
source: while slow versus miss trials were not (p=0.799)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: Behavioral responses were not predictable based on population dF/F0.
source: Behavioral responses were not predictable based on population dF/F0 (slow-miss, p=0.157; slow-fast, p=0.811; fast-miss, p=0.924)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: Detected stimuli (slow and fast responses) elicit a faster rise to the maximum heterogeneity level than undetected stimuli (miss trials).
source: detected stimuli (slow and fast responses) elicit a faster rise to the maximum heterogeneity level than undetected stimuli (miss trials) (paired t-tests, n=8 animals, p<0.05)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5f with statistical analysis.

claim: The population heterogeneity during stimulus presentation does not merely reflect a continuation of pre-stimulus neural state.
source: The population heterogeneity during stimulus presentation does not merely reflect a continuation of pre-stimulus neural state
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rise time analysis.

claim: The formation of nonhomogenous response patterns within neuronal populations is related to the actual detection of visual stimuli and constitutes a second effect in addition to background heterogeneity.
source: The formation of nonhomogenous response patterns within neuronal populations is also related to the actual detection of visual stimuli and constitutes a second effect in addition to background heterogeneity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined pre-stimulus and stimulus-evoked heterogeneity analyses.

claim: Within the preferred population, as well as within the nonpreferred population, neuronal population activity patterns were more similar during fast trials, with a trend for slow trials, than during miss trials.
source: Within the preferred population, as well as within the nonpreferred population, we found that neuronal population activity patterns were more similar during fast trials, with a trend for slow trials, than during miss trials (preferred population, miss-slow; p=0.081, miss-fast; p<0.05, nonpreferred population, miss-slow; p<0.05, miss-fast; p<0.05) (Figure 6c,d)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6c,d with statistical analysis.

claim: Population pattern correlations were significantly higher than shuffled for fast and slow trials, while miss trial consistency was not statistically different from the shuffled control.
source: Similarly, population pattern correlations were significantly higher than shuffled for fast and slow trials, while miss trial consistency was not statistically different from the shuffled control (both preferred and nonpreferred populations, paired t-tests shuffled vs. real, miss; p>0.3, slow and fast; p<0.05)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis comparing real to shuffled data.

claim: Pattern consistencies are relatively low and cannot fully account for the population activity structure.
source: However, note that these pattern consistencies are relatively low: they cannot fully account for the population activity structure and must therefore be interpreted as happening against a background of dynamic population activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the magnitude of the correlation values observed.

claim: The inter-point distance was slightly, but significantly larger for hit than miss trials.
source: The data show that the inter-point distance was slightly, but significantly larger for hit than miss trials (paired t-test, p<0.05) (Figure 7f)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7f with statistical analysis.

claim: Population responses during hits encompass a larger volume of neural response space than during misses.
source: This indicates that population responses during hits encompass a larger volume of neural response space than during misses, which will increase heterogeneity values and allows more information to be encoded with the same number of neurons.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the inter-point distance analysis.

claim: There was a small but significant increase in inter-point distance for both hits and misses when mirroring across the diagonal.
source: There was a small but significant increase in inter-point distance for both hits and misses
evidence: This is a statistical result from the mirroring analysis.

claim: Mirroring increased the inter-point distance more for hits than misses.
source: and mirroring increased the inter-point distance more for hits than misses (p<0.05; Figure 7f, inset)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7f inset with statistical analysis.

claim: Population responses during hit trials are more asymmetrical (i.e. more clustered in discrete states of neural activity) than during miss trials.
source: the difference between hits and misses suggests that population responses during hit trials are more asymmetrical (i.e. more clustered in discrete states of neural activity) than during miss trials (Figure 7f, inset)
evidence: This is an interpretation of the mirroring analysis results.

claim: Neuronal populations during miss trials show more random behavior within a limited neural space, while neuronal populations during hit trials show more structured behavior in a more extended neural space.
source: Considering that inter-trial population pattern consistencies were lower during miss trials (Figure 6), we can conclude that neuronal populations during miss trials show more random behavior within a limited neural space, while neuronal populations during hit trials show more structured behavior in a more extended neural space.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from combining multiple analyses.

claim: Removing heterogeneity led to a small but significant decrease in decoding performance compared to original data.
source: but removing heterogeneity (or both heterogeneity and the mean) led to a small but significant decrease in decoding performance (heterogeneity-removed vs. original data, p<0.05; heterogeneity-removed vs. mean-removed, p<0.05) (Figure 7h)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7h with statistical analysis.

claim: Even with heterogeneity removed, decoding performance was still well above chance.
source: However, even with heterogeneity removed, decoding performance was still well above chance (63% correct for original data, 60% correct for both removed; 50% is chance)
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the decoding analysis.

claim: Heterogeneity contributes significantly as a non-epiphenomal population property to the differentiation in neural responses between visual detections and failures to detect a stimulus.
source: We, therefore, conclude that heterogeneity contributes significantly as a non-epiphenomal population property to the differentiation in neural responses between visual detections and failures to detect a stimulus
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the multidimensional analysis.

claim: Most information resides in neuronal population response patterns other than its mean or heterogeneity.
source: but also that most information resides in neuronal population response patterns other than its mean or heterogeneity
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the decoding analysis showing above-chance performance even after removing mean and heterogeneity.

claim: The mean response of a neuronal population is less important than its heterogeneity.
source: Moreover, the mean response of a neuronal population is less important than its heterogeneity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the effects of removing mean versus heterogeneity.

claim: Behavioral stimulus detection correlates more with nonlinear neuronal population activation patterns, such as heterogeneity, correlations, and variance, rather than overall response strength in L2/3 of mouse V1.
source: We found that behavioral stimulus detection correlates more with nonlinear neuronal population activation patterns, such as heterogeneity, correlations, and variance, rather than overall response strength in L2/3 of mouse V1 (Figures 2 and 3; Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the study.

claim: The differentiation in activation within neuronal populations predicts visual detection, and particularly behavioral reaction time.
source: we show that the differentiation in activation within these populations predicts visual detection, and particularly behavioral reaction time
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the study.

claim: High heterogeneity is associated with an increased accuracy of stimulus presence and feature representation by the population.
source: and is associated with an increased accuracy of stimulus presence and feature representation by the population (Figure 4; Figure 4—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the decoding analysis.

claim: High heterogeneity prior to stimuli correlated with fast hit responses.
source: High heterogeneity prior to stimuli correlated with fast hit responses
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the pre-stimulus analysis.

claim: Detection-related population activity may be gated by arousal mechanisms.
source: indicating that detection-related population activity may be gated by arousal mechanisms (Figure 5; Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is an interpretation of the pre-stimulus heterogeneity findings.

claim: Neuronal population activation patterns are more similar during accurate task performance upon repetition of the same stimulus, but not when the animal fails to respond.
source: Neuronal population activation patterns are more similar during accurate task performance upon repetition of the same stimulus, but not when the animal fails to respond, suggesting that specific population patterns may recur when the animal is well engaged in the task (Figure 6)
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the inter-trial correlation analysis.

claim: Neural processing of information related to detection behavior depends on transient differentiation in neuronal activity within cortical populations rather than on temporally stable ensembles or on gain modulation of population activity as a whole.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that neural processing of information related to detection behavior depends on transient differentiation in neuronal activity within cortical populations rather than on temporally stable ensembles or on gain modulation of population activity as a whole (Figure 7)
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from all the analyses in the study.

claim: The relatively mild water restriction led to a behavioral performance at the 100% probe trials that is lower compared to other studies using similar tasks.
source: First, the relatively mild water restriction led to a behavioral performance at the 100% probe trials that is lower compared to other studies using similar tasks (Glickfeld et al., 2013)
evidence: This is an observation about the behavioral performance with a citation for comparison.

claim: During intermediate test contrasts (2% and 8%), the hit–miss difference in heterogeneity is largest.
source: Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1f,2 shows that this is not the case; during intermediate test contrasts (2% and 8%), the hit–miss difference in heterogeneity is largest
evidence: This is shown in the figures and described in the text.

claim: A heterogeneity difference between (false alarm) responses and correct rejections during 0% contrast probe trials was lacking.
source: A similar reasoning applies to 0% contrast probe trials, where a heterogeneity difference between (false alarm) responses and correct rejections was lacking
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: It is highly unlikely that the neural correlates of behavioral responses as reported in this study are due to differences in motivation.
source: Thus, it is highly unlikely that the neural correlates of behavioral responses as reported in this study are due to differences in motivation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the control analyses.

claim: Behavioral activity and running can induce instabilities in the plane of focus with awake two-photon calcium recordings, as well as changes in the neuronal responses in mouse V1.
source: it has been reported that behavioral activity and running can induce instabilities in the plane of focus with awake two-photon calcium recordings, as well as changes in the neuronal responses in mouse V1 (Dombeck et al., 2007; Niell and Stryker, 2010; Saleem et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies on imaging artifacts.

claim: Slight changes in z-location were detected after the onset of hit responses by licking, but these were mostly confined to the reward presentation period.
source: Slight changes in z-location were detected after the onset of hit responses by licking, but these were mostly confined to the reward presentation period (which was not used for any of our analyses) and rarely exceeded more than a couple of microns (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is shown in the supplementary figure and described in the text.

claim: Exclusion of trials where mice were running did not qualitatively change hit–miss differences in neuronal activity.
source: Moreover, exclusion of trials where mice were running did not qualitatively change hit–miss differences in neuronal activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1g,h)
evidence: This is shown in the supplementary figure with analysis.

claim: Using only the first 400 ms after stimulus onset to avoid licking-preparation feedback from other brain regions did not qualitatively change the results.
source: nor did using only the first 400 ms after stimulus onset to avoid licking-preparation feedback from other brain regions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1i, j)
evidence: This is shown in the supplementary figure with analysis.

claim: After removing all trials where the animals were making saccades or were blinking, no qualitative difference with the results observed previously was found.
source: After removing all trials where the animals were making saccades or were blinking, we again found no qualitative difference with the results we observed previously (Figure 2—figure supplement 1k,l)
evidence: This is shown in the supplementary figure with analysis.

claim: A small but significant correlation between pupil size and heterogeneity was observed, suggesting higher heterogeneity with increased arousal states.
source: but did observe a small but significant correlation between pupil size and heterogeneity, suggesting higher heterogeneity with increased arousal states (Figure 4—figure supplement 1e)
evidence: This is shown in the supplementary figure with analysis.

claim: The neural correlates reported are most likely not due to recording instability, changes in motivation, locomotion, motor-related signals associated with licking, or eye movements and blinking.
source: Overall, we conclude that the neural correlates we report here, and interpret as related to perception, are most likely not due to recording instability, changes in motivation, locomotion, motor-related signals associated with licking, or eye movements and blinking.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple control analyses.

claim: The results only pertain to L2/3 of the primary visual cortex in mouse.
source: Importantly, our results only pertain to L2/3 of the primary visual cortex in mouse
evidence: This is a statement about the scope and limitations of the study.

claim: Extensive differences exist between superficial and deep layers: whereas L2/3 neurons often show relatively low peak firing rates and sparse responses to sensory stimulation, L5 neurons show denser response patterns with on average higher peak firing rates.
source: Previous research has shown that extensive differences exist between superficial and deep layers: whereas L2/3 neurons often show relatively low peak firing rates and sparse responses to sensory stimulation, L5 neurons show denser response patterns with on average higher peak firing rates (De Kock and Sakmann, 2008; Harris and Mrsic-Flogel, 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on layer differences.

claim: In somatosensory cortex, hits and correct rejections in a go-no-go object localization task can be better separated using mean spiking rates in L5 than in L2/3.
source: In somatosensory cortex, it has been shown that hits and correct rejections in a go-no-go object localization task can be better separated using mean spiking rates in L5 than in L2/3 (O'Connor et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study in somatosensory cortex.

claim: The result that L2/3 populations show only a small differentiation between hit and miss responses in mean activation should not be taken as proof for a canonical principle also applicable to other cortical layers.
source: Our result that L2/3 populations show only a small differentiation between hit and miss responses in mean activation should therefore not be taken as proof for a canonical principle also applicable to other cortical layers.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations and generalizability of the findings.

claim: The observation that stimulus features are represented more accurately during hit than miss trials may be somewhat surprising given that orientation was task-irrelevant.
source: Our observation that stimulus features are represented more accurately (as quantified by decoding accuracy) during hit than miss trials may therefore be somewhat surprising (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a)
evidence: This is an interpretation of the decoding results in the context of the task design.

claim: Mechanisms that increase the likelihood of stimulus detection may be acting through a general enhancement of stimulus processing intensity.
source: This suggests that mechanisms that increase the likelihood of stimulus detection may be acting through a general enhancement of stimulus processing intensity, corroborating previous research in monkey showing that attention can lead to horizontal shifts in contrast response curves, as if the stimulus were of higher contrast (Martı́nez-Trujillo and Treue, 2002)
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings with support from a citation to prior research.

claim: Sparseness in L2/3 populations of rodent V1 is high during passive viewing and depends on cortical state.
source: Of further interest is to compare our results on heterogeneity with studies reporting that sparseness in L2/3 populations of rodent V1 is high during passive viewing (Barth and Poulet, 2012) depends on cortical state and improves neural discriminability during passive processing of natural scenes (Froudarakis et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies on sparseness.

claim: In the analysis, sparseness and variance explained more behavioral variability in reaction time than (z-scored) mean population activity.
source: Although in our analysis sparseness and variance explained more behavioral variability in reaction time than (z-scored) mean population activity (Figure 4c)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4c with analysis.

claim: Sparseness and variance perform much worse than heterogeneity and the spread of instantaneous Pearson-like correlations.
source: these measures perform much worse than heterogeneity and the spread of instantaneous Pearson-like correlations
evidence: This is a comparison of the performance of different metrics.

claim: A sample of ~60–70 tuned neurons may be insufficient to estimate instantaneous sparseness accurately.
source: Possibly, a sample of ~60–70 tuned neurons is insufficient to estimate instantaneous sparseness accurately.
evidence: This is a speculation about why sparseness performed poorly.

claim: Sparseness of L2/3 populations may result from anatomical wiring required for efficient stimulus coding and to enable locally selective synaptic plasticity without immediately changing the coding of stimulus features within the population response.
source: An alternative explanation for this poor correlation could be that sparseness of L2/3 populations results from anatomical wiring required for efficient stimulus coding and to enable locally selective synaptic plasticity without immediately changing the coding of stimulus features within the population response (Rao and Ballard, 1999)
evidence: This is a speculation with support from a citation to a theoretical paper.

claim: Sparse stimulus representation by L2/3 neurons reflects a structural optimization of the population code to represent stimulus features, while heterogeneity captures more temporally dynamic modulations related to perception.
source: This latter interpretation is in line with the data we recorded and suggests that sparse stimulus representation by L2/3 neurons reflects a structural optimization of the population code to represent stimulus features, while heterogeneity captures more temporally dynamic modulations related to perception.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the relationship between sparseness and heterogeneity.

claim: While heterogeneity is more important for separating stimulus detections from nondetection in neural response space than the population mean, these properties combined still cannot capture the full set of neuronal response characteristics that define the accurate detection of visual stimuli in L2/3 of mouse V1.
source: These results indicate that, while heterogeneity is more important for separating stimulus detections from nondetection in neural response space than the population mean, these properties combined still cannot capture the full set of neuronal response characteristics that define the accurate detection of visual stimuli in L2/3 of mouse V1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the multidimensional analysis.

claim: Other patterns of population activity, such as potentially transient assembly formation, may be important for visual stimuli to be correctly detected.
source: This suggests that other patterns of population activity, such as potentially transient assembly formation, may be important for visual stimuli to be correctly detected.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the incomplete explanatory power of mean and heterogeneity.

claim: Simple bulk approaches (i.e. correlating a population's mean response with behavioral output) are insufficient when one aims to address how early sensory cortex areas are involved in the processing and detection of visual stimuli.
source: From our multidimensional analyses, we can conclude that simple bulk approaches (i.e. correlating a population's mean response with behavioral output) are insufficient when one aims to address how early sensory cortex areas are involved in the processing and detection of visual stimuli.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall findings of the study.

claim: The observation of behavioral-state-specific consistencies in population activation patterns across trials provides some constraints on how population heterogeneity is modulated at a neurophysiological level.
source: Related to these findings is our observation of behavioral-state-specific consistencies in population activation patterns across trials. This provides some constraints on how population heterogeneity is modulated at a neurophysiological level.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the inter-trial correlation findings.

claim: Neuromodulators may facilitate repeated activation of similar subnetworks of neurons within a population responding to the same stimulus.
source: such that they facilitate repeated activation of similar subnetworks of neurons within a population responding to the same stimulus
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism underlying the observed pattern consistencies.

claim: Without neuromodulators, neurons within the same preferred population would randomly participate in representing the current stimulus.
source: Without such neuromodulators, neurons within the same preferred population would randomly participate in representing the current stimulus.
evidence: This is a speculation about what would happen without neuromodulators.

claim: ACh has been observed to influence burst spiking, membrane potential fluctuations, cortical oscillations, and desynchronization.
source: for instance, ACh has been observed to influence burst spiking, membrane potential fluctuations, cortical oscillations, and desynchronization
evidence: This is a statement about known effects of ACh based on the literature.

claim: These processes have been implicated in modulating competitive inhibition effects within neuronal populations and may very well influence the consistency of specific neuronal subnetworks being activated.
source: These processes have been implicated in modulating competitive inhibition effects within neuronal populations and may very well influence the consistency of specific neuronal subnetworks being activated (Borgers et al., 2008; Fries, 2009; Bosman et al., 2014)
evidence: This is a speculation with support from citations to prior research.

claim: If heterogeneity in a recurrently connected V1 population is in part determined by suppression of the most weakly by the most strongly stimulus-driven neurons, then behaviorally correlated heterogeneity enhancements may be another facet of arousal as well as perception-related modulations of stimulus-evoked population activity.
source: If heterogeneity in a recurrently connected V1 population is in part determined by suppression of the most weakly by the most strongly stimulus-driven neurons, then behaviorally correlated heterogeneity enhancements may be another facet of arousal as well as perception-related modulations of stimulus-evoked population activity.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism underlying heterogeneity.

claim: Population heterogeneity is correlated with behavioral stimulus detection and predicts correct behavioral performance.
source: Here, we show that population heterogeneity is correlated with behavioral stimulus detection and that it predicts correct behavioral performance.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: Neurophysiological measures dependent on population averages (i.e. multiunit activity, EEG, and fMRI) may underestimate the correlation between visual detection and V1 L2/3 activity because the assumption of population response homogeneity is violated especially during active processing of visual information.
source: Our results imply that neurophysiological measures dependent on population averages (i.e. multiunit activity, EEG, and fMRI) may underestimate the correlation between visual detection and V1 L2/3 activity because the assumption of population response homogeneity is violated especially during active processing of visual information.
evidence: This is an implication of the findings for interpreting other types of measurements.

claim: The results support contrast-sensitive changes in mean population activity during visual task performance.
source: In short, our results support contrast-sensitive changes in mean population activity during visual task performance (Figure 3c,d)
evidence: This is a summary statement about one aspect of the findings.

claim: The results stress the importance of population recordings with single-cell resolution.
source: but stress the importance of population recordings with single-cell resolution (Figure 4c–f)
evidence: This is a conclusion about the methodological implications of the findings.
